en: Dhammasaṅgaṇī:
The Dyad Matrix,
the Section on Causes (Hetugocchaka)
1. The Dyad on Causes: Phenomena that are causes. (1059, 1077, 1441) Phenomena that are not causes. (1078, 1442)
2. The Dyad of With-Root-Causes: States with root-causes.
(1079, 1443) States without root-causes. (1080, 1444)
3. The Dyads on Association with Roots States associated with roots.
(1081, 1445) States dissociated from roots. (1082, 1446)
4. The Dyad of Causes and Having-Causes States that are both causes and having-causes.
(1083, 1447) States that are having-causes but are not causes. (1084, 1448)
5. The Dyad of Causes and Factors Associated with Causes States that are both causes and associated with causes.
(1085, 1449) States that are associated with causes but are not causes. (1086, 1450)
6. The Dyads on Non-Roots and With-Roots:
Furthermore, states that are not roots may be with-root, and they may also be rootless.
The Group on Causes (Hetugocchaka).
The Minor Intermediate Dyads (Cūḷantaraduka) 1.
The Dyad on Conditioned (Sappaccayaduka).
States with conditions. (1089, 1453) States without conditions.
(1090, 1454) 2. The Dyad of the Conditioned.
Conditioned phenomena.
(1091, 1455) Unconditioned phenomena.
(1092, 1456) 3. The Dyad of the Visible.
Dharmas with visibility. (1093, 1457) Dharmas without visibility.
(1094, 1458) 4. The Dyad of the Impinging.
Dharmas with resistance. (1095, 1459) Dharmas without resistance. (1096, 1460) 5.
The dyad of material form.
Material phenomena. (1097, 1461) Immaterial phenomena.
(1098, 1462) 6. The Dyad of the Mundane.
Worldly phenomena. (1099, 1463) Supramundane phenomena.
(1100, 1464) 7. The Dyad of Being Cognizable by Someone.
States cognizable by something;
(1101, 1464) states not cognizable by something.
The Minor Intermediate Dyad.
The Group on the Taints (Āsavagocchaka). 1. The Dyad on the Taints: The taints are phenomena. (1102, 1465)
States that are without taints (*anāsava*).
(1107, 1466) 2. The Group on States with Taints (*sāsava*): States that are with taints (*sāsava*). (1108, 1467)
States free from taints.
(1109, 1468) 3. The dyad of states associated with taints: States associated with taints. (1110, 1469)
States dissociated from the taints.
The dyad of taints and states with taints: States that are both taints and associated with taints. (1112, 1471)
Dharmas that are both associated with the taints (*āsava*) and not themselves taints.
(1113, 1472) 5. The dyad of taints and dharmas associated with taints:
Dharmas that are both taints and associated with taints. (1114, 1473)
States that are associated with the taints but are not themselves taints.
(1115, 1474) 6. The dyad of states dissociated from the taints yet subject to the taints:
Furthermore, states that are dissociated from the taints may also be subject to the taints. (1116, 1475)
Also those without taints.
(1117, 1476) The Chapter on Taints.
The Chapter on Fetters.
1. The Dyad of Fetters:
Phenomena that are fetters.
(1118, 1477) Phenomena that are not fetters. (1129, 1478)
2. The Dyad of Things that Conduce to Fettering: Phenomena that conduce to fettering;
phenomena that do not conduce to fettering. (1130, 1479) (1131, 1480)
3. The Dyad of Factors Associated with the Fetters. Factors associated with the fetters.
(1132, 1481) Factors dissociated from the fetters. (1133, 1482)
4. The Dyad of Fetters and the Fetterable. (1134, 1483) States that are both fetters and fetterable.
(1135, 1484) States that are fetterable but are not fetters.
5. The Dyad of Fetters and Association with Fetters States that are both fetters and associated with fetters.
(1136, 1485) States that are associated with fetters but are not themselves fetters. (1137, 1486)
6. The Dyad of Factors Dissociated from Fettering but Subject to Fettering.
Furthermore, those factors dissociated from fetters are both subject to fettering and not subject to fettering.
(1138, 1487) They are also not subject to fettering. (1139, 1488)
The Group on Fettering (Saññojanagocchaka).
The Group on Ties (Ganthagocchaka) 1.
The Dyad on Ties (Ganthaduka).
States that are fetters. (1140, 1489) States that are not fetters.
(1145, 1490) 2. The Dyad of the Fetterable.
States that are subject to the fetters.
(1146, 1491) States that are not subject to the fetters.
(1147, 1492) 3. The Dyad of States Associated with the Fetters.
States associated with the ties.
(1148, 1493) States dissociated from the ties.
(1149, 1494) 4. The Dyad of Ties and that which is Tied.
States that are both fetters and objects of the fetters.
(1150, 1495) States that are objects of the fetters but are not themselves fetters.
(1151, 1496) 5. The Dyads on Fettering and Being Associated with Fetters.
Both the fetters themselves and those phenomena associated with the fetters.
(1152, 1497) Those phenomena associated with the fetters but which are not themselves fetters.
(1153, 1498) 6. The dyad of those dissociated from the fetters and subject to the fetters.
Furthermore, states dissociated from the ties are both subject to the ties and not subject to the ties.
(1154, 1499; 1155, 1500) The Group on Ties is finished.
The Flood Section.
1. The Dyad on Floods: States that are floods. (1156, 1501)
Not-flood phenomena.
2. The Dyad of Flood-Entailing:
Flood-entailing phenomena.
States that are not subject to the floods.
3. The dyad of states associated with the floods:
states associated with the floods.
States dissociated from the floods. 4. The Floods and the States Subject to the Floods (Ogha-oghaniya-duka):
Those states which are both floods and subject to the floods.
States that are floods but are not themselves the flood.
5. The Dyads on Floods and Association with Floods:
States that are both floods and associated with the flood.
States that are associated with the floods but are not themselves floods.
6. The dyad of states dissociated from the floods yet subject to the floods:
furthermore, states dissociated from the floods may also be subject to the floods.
The *Anoghaniya* [Chapter].
The *Oghagocchaka*.
The *Yogagocchaka*.
1. The Pair on Fetters:
States that are fetters;
states that are not fetters.
2. The Dyad of the Conducive to Yoga:
Phenomena conducive to yoga;
phenomena not conducive to yoga.
3. The Pair on States Associated with Yoga: States associated with yoga;
states dissociated from yoga.
4. The dyad of factors that are both yokes and bound by the yoke, and factors that are bound by the yoke but are not themselves yokes.
Factors that are both yokes and bound by the yoke. Factors that are bound by the yoke but are not themselves yokes.
5. The Dyad of States Both Associated with the Yokes and Conjoined with the Yokes; States Conjoined with the Yokes but Not the Yokes Themselves.
States that are both yokes and conjoined with the yokes; states that are conjoined with the yokes but are not themselves yokes.
6. The dyad of factors dissociated from the yokes and those that are conducive to the yokes:
Furthermore, states dissociated from the yokes are both conducive to the yokes and not conducive to the yokes.
The Group on Yoga.
The Group on Hindrances.
1. The Dyad on Hindrances.
States that are hindrances.
(1158, 1503) States that are not hindrances. (1169, 1504) 2. The Dyad of Hindrance-Worthy States.
States that are subject to hindrances.
(1170, 1505) States that are not subject to hindrances. (1171, 1506) 3. The dyad of states associated with hindrances.
States associated with the hindrances.
(1172, 1507) States dissociated from the hindrances. (1173, 1508) 4. The Dyad of Hindrances and the State of Being Hindered by Hindrances.
States that are both hindrances and subject to hindrance.
(1174, 1509) States that are subject to hindrance but are not themselves hindrances. (1175, 1510) 5. The dyad of states that are hindrances and associated with hindrances.
States that are both hindrances and associated with hindrances.
(1176, 1511) States that are associated with hindrances but are not themselves hindrances.
(1177, 1512) 6. The Dyad of States Dissociated from Hindrances but Subject to Hindrances.
Furthermore, states dissociated from the hindrances may be subject to the hindrances, and they may also not be subject to the hindrances.
(1178, 1513) (1179, 1514) This concludes the Group on Hindrances (*nīvaraṇagocchaka*).
The Group on Misapprehension 1.
The Dyad on Misapprehension: States that are misapprehensions. (1180, 1515)
(1182, 1516) 1. Non-perverted states.
Perverted states. Perverted states.
States that are not adhered to.
(1184, 1518) 3. The Dyad of States Associated with Adherence: States associated with adherence. (1185, 1519)
States dissociated from the perversions.
(1186, 1520) 4. The Dyad of Perversions and States Grasped by Perversions: States that are both perversions and grasped by perversions. (1187, 1521)
(1188, 1522) There are phenomena that are adhered to but are not themselves perversions.
(1189, 1523) Furthermore, there are phenomena dissociated from perversions that are nevertheless adhered to. This is the dyad of "dissociated from perversions but adhered to."
Also not grasped. (1190, 1524) The Group on Grasping.
The Great Intermediate Dyads.
1. The Pair on Having an Object: States with an object.
(1191, 1525) States without an object. (1192, 1526)
2. The Dyad of Consciousness: Mental states that are consciousness. (1193, 1527) Mental states that are not consciousness. (1194, 1528)
3. The Pair on Mental Factors (Cetasikaduka): Mental factors (cetasika-dhammā).
(1195, 1529) Non-mental factors (acetasika-dhammā). (1196, 1530)
4. The Pair of Factors Associated with Mind (*cittasampayuttaduka*): Factors associated with mind (*cittasampayuttā dhammā*).
(1197, 1531) Factors dissociated from mind (*cittavippayuttā dhammā*). (1198, 1532)
5. The Dyad on Conjoined with Mind: Phenomena conjoined with mind;
phenomena not conjoined with mind. (1199, 1533) (1200, 1534)
6. The Dyad on Mind-Origination:
States originated by mind; states not originated by mind.
7. The Pair on Coexistence with Consciousness:
Phenomena that coexist with consciousness;
(1203, 1537) phenomena that do not coexist with consciousness. (1204, 1538)
8. The Dyad on Concomitance with Mind States that are concomitant with mind.
(1205, 1539) States that are not concomitant with mind. (1206, 1540)
9. The Dyad of Conjoined and Originated by Mind:
States that are conjoined with and originated by mind;
(1207, 1541) states that are not conjoined with and originated by mind. (1208, 1542)

10. The Dyads of Being Conjoined With, Arisen From, and Co-existent With Mind; and Not Being Conjoined With, Arisen From, and Co-existent With Mind. (1209, 1543) States that are conjoined with, arisen from, and co-existent with mind.
(1210, 1544) States that are not conjoined with, arisen from, and co-existent with mind.
11. The Dyad of Factors Conjoined With, Arisen From, and Following Along With the Mind. Factors conjoined with, arisen from, and following along with the mind.
(1211, 1545) Factors not conjoined with, arisen from, and following along with the mind. (1212, 1546)
12. The Internal Dyad: Internal phenomena. (1213, 1547) External phenomena. (1214, 1548)
13. Derived. Derived phenomena. (1215, 1549) Non-derived phenomena. (1216, 1550)
14. The Dyad of Appropriated Phenomena: Appropriated phenomena.
(1217, 1551) Non-appropriated phenomena. (1218, 1552)
The Great Pair.
The Group on Grasping 1.
The Pair on Grasping.
States that are objects of clinging.
(1219, 1553) States that are not objects of clinging. (1224, 1554) 2. The Dyad of States Subject to Clinging.
States that are subject to clinging.
(1225, 1555) States that are not subject to clinging. (1226, 1556) 3. The Dyad of States Associated with Clinging.
States associated with clinging.
(1227, 1557) States dissociated from clinging.
(1228, 1558) 4. The Dyad of Clinging and the Objects of Clinging.
States that are both clinging and objects of clinging.
(1229, 1559) States that are objects of clinging but are not clinging.
(1230, 1560) 5. The Dyads on Clinging and Association with Clinging.
(1231, 1561) States that are both clinging and associated with clinging.
(1232, 1562) States that are associated with clinging but are not clinging.
6. The Dyad of Being Dissociated from Clinging yet Subject to Clinging.
Furthermore, states dissociated from clinging are both subject to clinging and not subject to clinging.
(1233, 1563) (1234, 1564) This concludes the Group on Clinging.
The Group on Defilements 1.
The Dyad on Defilements: Defilements are phenomena. (1235, 1565)
States that are defilements.
(1246, 1566) 2. The Dyad of Corruptible States: States that are corruptible. (1247, 1567)
States that are not subject to defilement.
(1248, 1568) 3. The Pair of Defiled States: Defiled states. (1249, 1569)
Un-defiled phenomena. (1250, 1570) 4.
The Dyad of Factors Associated with Defilements: Phenomena associated with defilements. (1251, 1571)
States dissociated from the defilements.
(1252, 1572) 5. The Dyad of Defilements and Corrupt States: States that are both defilements and corrupt. (1253, 1573)
States that are defiled but are not themselves defilements.
(1254, 1574) 6. The Dyad of Defilements and Defiled States: States that are both defilements and defiled. (1255, 1575)
States that are defiled but are not themselves defilements.
(1256, 1576) 7. The Dyad of Defilements and States Associated with Defilements: States that are both defilements and associated with defilements. (1257, 1577)
States that are associated with the defilements but are not themselves defilements.
(1258, 1578) 8. The Dyad of States Dissociated from Defilements yet Subject to Defilement:
Furthermore, states that are dissociated from the defilements may also be subject to defilement. (1259, 1579)
Also non-defiled. (1260, 1580) The Group on Defilements.
The Subsequent Dyads.
1. The Dyad of States to be Abandoned by Seeing: States to be abandoned by seeing. (1261, 1581) States not to be abandoned by seeing. (1265, 1582)
2. The Pair on States to be Abandoned by Cultivation: States to be abandoned by cultivation. (1266, 1583) States not to be abandoned by cultivation. (1267, 1584)
3. The Dyad of Factors to be Abandoned by Seeing States whose causes are to be abandoned by seeing. (1268, 1585) States whose causes are not to be abandoned by seeing. (1272, 1586)
4. The Dyads on Roots to be Abandoned by Cultivation:
States whose roots are to be abandoned by cultivation.
(1273, 1587) States whose roots are not to be abandoned by cultivation. (1274, 1588)
5. The Dyad of With-Initial-Application: Dhammas with initial application;
dhammas without initial application. (1275, 1589) (1276, 1590)
6. The Pair of With-Investigation:
Phenomena with investigation;
(1277, 1591) phenomena without investigation. (1278, 1592)
7. The Dyad of With Rapture:
(1279, 1593) States with rapture;
(1280, 1594) states without rapture.
8. The Dyad Associated with Rapture States associated with rapture;
states not associated with rapture.
9. The Dyads Associated with Pleasure:
Phenomena associated with pleasure;
phenomena not associated with pleasure.
10. The Pair Concerning Accompanied by Equanimity: States accompanied by equanimity. (1285, 1599) States not accompanied by equanimity. (1286, 1600)
11. The Dyad of Sense-Sphere Phenomena: Sense-sphere phenomena.
(1287, 1601) Non-sense-sphere phenomena. (1288, 1602)
12. The Dyad of the Form-Sphere. Form-sphere phenomena. (1289, 1603) Non-form-sphere phenomena. (1290, 1604)
13. The Pair on the Formless Realm:
Formless-sphere phenomena.
(1291, 1605) Non-formless-sphere phenomena. (1292, 1606)
14. The Pair on the Included (Pariyāpannaduka):
States that are included (pariyāpanna).
(1293, 1607) States that are not included (apariyāpanna). (1294, 1608)
15. The Dyad on Leading Out States that lead out;
(1295, 1609) states that do not lead out. (1296, 1610)
16. The Pair on the Determined: Determined phenomena.
(1297, 1611) Undetermined phenomena. (1298, 1612)
17. The Pairs with Superior and the Unsurpassed. (1299, 1613) Dhammas with superior; (1300, 1614) unsurpassed dhammas.
18. The Pair on Conflict (*saraṇaduka*).
States with conflict (*saraṇā dhammā*). (1301, 1615).
States without conflict (*araṇā dhammā*). (1302, 1616).
The Posterior Dyads.
The Matrix of the Abhidhamma Dyads.
